Abu Mojtaba al-Yasiri, a commander in the Islamic Resistance in Iraq, an umbrella group of Iran-backed armed factions, described the US withdrawal as "a historic victory for the Iraqi Islamic resistance groups and honourable Iraqis, and a crushing defeat for the American project". "On Sep 30, we will celebrate the turning of a black page in Iraq’s history and the failure of the occupation to impose its will on our country," he told Reuters. "Iraq has proven that its sovereignty cannot be secured by foreign forces, but by the resistance and the will of its people." NOT READY While the eventual departure of US forces is broadly popular among Iraqis, those who worry about the strength of the Iran-backed groups fear the withdrawal is premature. "We believe Iraq is still not fully ready to take over the security file at this time," Abdulrahman al-Zobaie, a Sunni tribal leader in Fallujah, once a bastion of anti-American resistance, told Reuters. "All Iraqis aspire to full sovereignty, and no Iraqi would dispute that. But I believe that the (US-led coalition) leaving in this way and creating a vacuum is what all Iraqis fear." American forces invaded Iraq in 2003 to topple Sunni Muslim dictator Saddam Hussein, and went on to occupy the country, install a Shi'ite-led government and fight a years-long counterinsurgency before withdrawing at the end of 2011. They returned less than three years later to help Iraqi forces defeat the Sunni militant group Islamic State in a major war from 2014 to 2017. Around twice as many Americans died in "Operation Iraqi Freedom" as in the parallel war in Afghanistan, which ended with an abrupt US withdrawal in 2021. In recent years, Iraq has been the only country to maintain close political and military alliances with both the United States and Iran, which sometimes used Iraqi territory as a proxy battlefield. The United States killed a top Iranian commander, Qasem Soleimani, with a strike on Baghdad Airport in 2020. Iran's allies repeatedly fired on US bases, sometimes drawing reprisals. In this year's war against Iran, 7 of the 18 US service members listed as killed were in Iraq, the last an army sergeant who died during the controlled detonation of a drone at a base near Erbil in July.

Related:

Trump expects new Iran talks despite rejecting deal offer

Iran supreme leader says US will be forced out of Middle East

VICTORY FOR IRAN'S AXIS Iran, which says its ultimate aim is to force American forces to leave the entire Middle East, casts the US withdrawal from Iraq as a victory for its "axis of resistance" of allied armed groups across the region. "Lasting security will prevail in Iraq" once the Americans leave the country and the region, the deputy chairman of the National Security Commission of Iran's Parliament, Amir Hayat Moqaddam, said on Monday. Iran "welcomes the withdrawal of American troops from Iraq and will undoubtedly support it", he told Iran's parliamentary news service. "Resistance groups are currently taking action, sometimes targeting and confronting American troops." Washington has accused Iran-backed militia groups in Iraq of playing a role in the wider Middle East conflict by launching attacks on neighbouring countries at the direction of Tehran, most recently hitting a major Saudi oil pipeline this month. The Baghdad government says it is trying to curb their influence. NEW LIFE FOR ISLAMIC STATE? Some Iraqi security officials, both in the federal government and the semi-autonomous northern Kurdish region, say the US pullout also risks giving new life to Islamic State fighters, who, despite the defeat of their self-proclaimed caliphate nearly a decade ago, retain a sleeper cell network. At their height, the fighters occupied a third of Iraq and killed thousands of people, including hundreds they videotaped themselves gunning down inside a former US military base. A lack of US intelligence, logistical support and drones will give Islamic State a chance to regroup, said Kurdish commander Sirwan Barzani. "For more than two weeks, we have noticed movement by (Islamic State) sleeper cells, after it was announced in the general media that there will be an official withdrawal of the international coalition from Iraq by the end of September," he said. "This has boosted, in my opinion, the morale" of the fighters. Iraqi security forces said a suspected Islamic State cell was preparing suicide attacks to coincide with the pullout. The plot highlighted concerns that the militant group remains capable of exploiting security gaps despite years of military setbacks, said four Iraqi security and army officials. Islamic State "is seeking to send a message that the group is still powerful and capable of launching bloody attacks", said Colonel Khalid al-Bayati, a senior security official in the strategic oil town of Kirkuk.

Six big takeaways from a turbulent week of UN diplomacy

item.title: スイス金融市場監督機構、ジュリアス・ベアに対する執行手続き終える
item.description:
（ブルームバーグ）： スイスの富裕層向け資産運用会社ジュリアス・ベア・グループは29日、スイス金融市場監督機構（FINMA）が同社に対する執行手続きを終了したと発表した。ジュリアス・ベアはまた、自社株買いの承認を申請した。
「FINMAが一本化した執行手続きを終了したときょう発表した」と同社は資料で説明し、「この手続きは、以前のプライベートデット事業で発生した大規模な信用事案のほか、マネーロンダリング（資金洗浄）対策（AML）分野における特定の顧客グループに関連した過去の案件を対象としていた」とコメントした。
シュテファン・ボリンジャー最高経営責任者（CEO）は資料で「重要な節目に到達した」と表明。ジュリアス・ベアは「自社株買いプログラムに関する申請をFINMAに提出しており、最終承認待ちであることを確認した」とも明らかにした。
原題：Swiss Regulator Finma Ends Proceeding

item.title: 米国、カナダ産酒類や二輪車の輸入禁止を発動－貿易摩擦激化
item.description: （ブルームバーグ）：
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded:
（ブルームバーグ）： 米国がカナダ製品の一部に対し輸入禁止措置を発動した。両国の貿易戦争が一段と激化した格好だ。

カナダのカーニー政権が一部の米国製品に報復関税を課したことへの対抗措置として、米トランプ政権はカナダ産の二輪自動車と酒類、乳清（ホエイ）製品の輸入を禁止する。米東部時間29日午前0時1分（日本時間同午後1時1分）に発効した。

米国とカナダは長年の同盟国で、世界最長の国境を挟んで生産サプライチェーンが深く結び付いている。今回の輸入禁止措置は、両国間で激化する貿易摩擦の新たな一手となる。

カナダのノバスコシア銀行の経済部門が今月公表した試算によると、今回の輸入禁止措置の対象となる貿易額は約10億ドル（約1570億円）と比較的小さい。米国とカナダの2025年の財・サービス貿易額は約9000億ドルに上る。

ホワイトハウスは今月、今回の輸入禁止措置のほか、カナダから輸入する一部のチーズ製品やモーターボート、ゴルフカート、家具など複数の品目に50%の関税を課した。

これに先立ち、トランプ政権は8月22日、関税法338条に基づきカナダ製品の一部に50%の関税を発動。これを受け、カナダは9月8日に一部の米国製品に対する報復関税を発動していた。

トランプ氏は28日、カナダ当局が今後3－4週間以内に米国製品への関税を引き下げ、「謝罪」するとの見通しを示した。

これに対し、カーニー首相と閣僚らは、不利な合意を急いで結ぶ考えはないと表明している。カナダ政府はここ数カ月、欧州やアジアとの貿易網の拡大にも動いている。

原題：US Import Ban on Canadian Alcohol, Motorcycles Takes Effect (1)（抜粋）

item.title: エヌビディア､アンソロピックのCEOがトランプ氏と昼食会へ－AI議題に
item.description: （ブルームバーグ）：
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded:
（ブルームバーグ）： AIのリスクを話し合うトランプ米大統領との昼食会に、米半導体大手エヌビディアのジェンスン・フアン最高経営責任者（CEO）、米AI開発企業アンソロピックのダリオ・アモデイCEO、米ソフトウエア開発企業パランティア・テクノロジーズのアレックス・カープCEOが出席する予定だ。

昼食会はトランプ氏がジョンソン下院議長と29日に開くもので、米OpenAIのグレッグ・ブロックマン社長も出席する見通し。事情に詳しい関係者が明らかにした。出席予定者については、ニュースサイトのセマフォーと経済専門局CNBCが先に報じていた。

昼食会は、AIが人間に脅威をもたらすとの懸念が強まるなかで開かれる。アモデイ氏ら一部のAI業界幹部は、こうした懸念を踏まえ、技術開発のペースを落とすよう提唱している。

アモデイ氏は27日夜、トランプ氏と会談した。AIの安全性をめぐり立場の異なる二人が顔を合わせた。アモデイ氏は28日に連邦議会議事堂で、共和党のスーン上院院内総務を訪問。トランプ氏との会談について記者から問われたが、質問には答えなかった。ホワイトハウスとアンソロピックも内容を明らかにしていない。

ジョンソン氏は今月、AI業界から相次ぐ深刻な警告を受け、議会が「場合によっては」一定のガードレール（歯止め）を設ける必要があるとの考えを示した。一方、幅広い支持を得て法案を可決させるには「しばらく時間」がかかるとの見方も示した。

議員からはAIの安全性を確保するための複数の案が出ている。米下院のモラン議員（共和）とリュー議員（民主）は、制御不能になったシステムを停止できる仕組みを開発企業に義務づける措置を提案。別の超党派法案は、最先端モデルについて独立した安全性評価を義務づける内容だ。

上院では、民主党と行動をともにする無所属のバーニー・サンダース議員が、人間の制御を逃れるほど強力な超知能AIの開発禁止を提案している。

item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded:
（ブルームバーグ）： ANAホールディングス傘下の全日本空輸（ANA）は、上級会員向けのクレジットカード「ANAスーパーフライヤーズカード（SFC）」について、年間決済額が300万円未満の場合、混雑時には一部のラウンジを利用できなくする方針を明らかにした。

SFCは、上級会員の資格を得た顧客との関係を長期的に維持する仕組みとして機能してきた。会員数は2019年比で約1.5倍に増える一方、カードの利用金額は年々縮小している。ANAは会員の囲い込みを維持しながら、ラウンジなどのサービス品質をどう確保するかという課題に直面している。

発表によると、混雑時に入室できなくなるのは国内線の「ANA LOUNGE」。混雑緩和に向け、対象となる国内線ラウンジには将来的に事前予約制を導入する。一方、国内線の共用ラウンジや成田空港の「ANA ARRIVAL LOUNGE」、国際線で同社が運営する羽田、成田、ホノルルのラウンジはこれまで通り利用できる。

ANAによると、ANA LOUNGEは国内線向けでは羽田、新千歳、仙台、小松、伊丹、岡山、広島、松山、福岡、鹿児島、那覇空港の計11カ所にある。

ANAは4月、28年4月からSFCに年間のANAカードとANA Payの決済額に応じて2つの区分を設定すると発表した。年間決済額300万円以上の「SFC PLUS」ではラウンジを含め各種サービスを維持する一方、300万円未満の「SFC LITE」ではラウンジを利用できず、スターアライアンスの資格もシルバー会員に変更する内容だった。

この発表を巡っては、SNSでは「改悪」などとする批判の声が相次ぎ、ANAは6月に見直しを検討すると表明していた。今回の方針では、300万円未満でもラウンジ利用を全面的に制限せず、混雑時に対象を絞る。

ANAによると、SFC会員の4割は年間利用額が100万円未満で、約3割は50万円未満。カードの利用金額が年々縮小する一方、会員数は毎年増加しているという。

item.title: Myanmar arrests 21 over alleged donations to opposition-linked fundraising platform
item.description: Myanmar's military-backed government has arrested 21 people it said had transferred money to an online fundraising platform linked to the opposition National Unity Government (NUG), the state-run Global New Light of Myanmar newspaper reported.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Myanmar's military-backed government has arrested 21 people it said had transferred money to an online fundraising platform linked to the opposition National Unity Government (NUG), the state-run Global New Light of Myanmar newspaper reported. Here are some details: The state media report said authorities had identified the details of more than 2,700 people who allegedly provided financial support to the People's Revolution Supply Family (PRF) website, which was established by the NUG. The arrested individuals live in townships in Myanmar and will face legal action. The report said investigations will continue, while financial accounts linked to the funding will be closed and confiscated. Myanmar has faced political turmoil and conflict since a [USN:L4N3XR00I TEXT:"military coup"] overthrew a civilian government led by Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi in February 2021. A parallel civilian administration, the [USN:L1N2M90IC TEXT:"National Unity Government"], comprises remnants of Aung San Suu Kyi's party and anti-coup groups. In a statement issued late on Tuesday, the PRF said that it neither collects nor stores the personal information of people that support its activities. "Therefore, the allegation that information on more than 2,700 members had been obtained is baseless," it said. "It is clear that the primary purpose of these allegations is to intimidate the public, undermine trust in the PRF, and cut off the revolution's sources of income," the PRF added. The NUG-aligned People's Defence Force and ethnic armed organizations [USN:L4N4410HN TEXT:"have been fighting"] military forces across the country. After the coup, the junta designated the NUG and its allies as "[USN:L4N2UW0V2 TEXT:"terrorist organisations"]". The new military-backed government, which is headed by the former junta chief, has [USN:L4N43X0HL TEXT:"dismissed"] the regional ASEAN bloc's peace plan to end the fighting. Opposition groups have long used unofficial payment channels, online fundraising, cryptocurrency and bond sales to raise funds outside Myanmar's military-controlled banking system. Diaspora communities play a major role in supporting opposition groups, providing financial support through overseas transfers and alternative payment channels.

item.title: 円キャリー取引の巻き戻し、世界的な債券売りを加速も－ヤルデニ氏
item.description: （ブルームバーグ）：
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded:
（ブルームバーグ）： 円で資金を調達するキャリー取引を手掛けてきた投資家の動きが、世界的な債券売りを加速させている可能性があると、ヤルデニ・リサーチが指摘した。

同社のエド・ヤルデニ社長兼チーフ投資ストラテジストはリポートで、「世界的な債券相場の急落については、日本銀行が政策金利を引き上げる中で進む円キャリー取引の巻き戻しがより有力な要因とみられる。キャリー取引を手掛ける投資家は、低金利の円借り入れで調達した資金を使って購入した世界各国の国債の売却を迫られている」と分析した。

そのうえで、「この取引によって、多くの政府は国債利回りに上昇圧力をかけることなく財政赤字を膨らませることができた。今、そのツケが回ってきた」とした。

ヤルデニ氏によると、日銀や他の主要中央銀行が借り入れコストを異例の低水準に抑えていた時期に、各国政府は多額の債務を積み上げつつ巨額の財政赤字を計上した。

ヤルデニ氏は、「主要中央銀行が講じた量的緩和政策は世界の債券市場をゆがめ、債券自警団の動きを抑えた」と指摘した。

市場では現在、債券自警団の「復讐（ふくしゅう）」が起きている可能性があるという。

item.title: Tata shares slip as trusts' proposal clouds Tata Sons listing prospects
item.description: Tata group shares fell on Tuesday after the controlling charities proposed a restructuring of the holding company to prevent a central-bank-mandated listing, disappointing some investors.
item.dc:creator: Kashish Tandon
item.content:encoded: Tata group shares fell on Tuesday after the controlling charities proposed a restructuring of the holding company to prevent a central-bank-mandated listing, disappointing some investors. A group of Tata charities collectively known as Tata Trusts on Monday proposed [USN:L4N45K0YX TEXT:"merging"] two group entities with Tata Sons, the principal holding company of the salt-to-software conglomerate. Tata Trusts and the holding company have [USN:L4N45F0E6 TEXT:"been at odds"] over the [USN:L4N4590PM TEXT:"re-appointment"] of N Chandrasekaran as chairman and on a path to comply with the mandate to list after the Reserve Bank of India rejected Tata Sons' request to give up its registration as a so-called upper-layer non-banking finance company. The proposal dampens expectations of a listing that had gathered momentum, analysts said. "A listing was expected to unlock value for shareholders of Tata group companies that own stakes in Tata Sons, particularly Tata Chemicals and Tata Investment Corp," said Neeraj Dewan, an independent market analyst in New Delhi. "However, the reaction is largely sentiment-driven for now, as the proposal would still require approval from both (the board of) Tata Sons and the RBI, which has so far maintained its direction for the company to list." Tata Sons did not immediately respond to Reuters request for comment. Shares of Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles (TAMO.NS) fell 2% in Mumbai, while Tata Investment Corp (TINV.NS) lost 2.1% and Tata Chemicals (TTCH.NS) shed 3.1%. Trent (TREN.NS) and Tata Consultancy Services (TCS.NS) were down about 1% each. Tata Sons owns significant stakes in TCS, Tata Motors, Tata Steel and Trent. So far this year, TCS has lagged group shares, slumping nearly 35% amid IT sector woes. India's benchmark Nifty 50 index has fallen 13.5% over the same period.

item.title: Emotional Burnham sets out long-term vision to tackle UK’s woes
item.description: Prime Minister Andy Burnham pledged on Tuesday to revive Britain by tackling its deepest problems such as social care, housing and utilities — issues, he conceded, would take time to fix in what he described as an "honest" speech to the nation.
item.dc:creator: Elizabeth Piper, Alistair Smout, Andrew Macaskill
item.content:encoded: Prime Minister [USN:L8N43L03M TEXT:"Andy Burnham"] pledged on Tuesday to revive Britain by tackling its deepest problems such as social care, housing and utilities — issues, he conceded, would take time to fix in what he described as an "honest" speech to the nation. In an emotional address to his Labour Party in which he imagined the country his father, who died this month, would have wanted to see, Burnham set out a long-term vision, promising greater public control of utilities, reform of the so-called [USN:L8N45L1L9 TEXT:"pensions triple lock"] and the construction of more social housing. Yet, the former Greater Manchester mayor, 56, said he could only start setting out the groundwork for resolving those priorities, constrained in the near term by stretched public finances and the previous government's tax pledges. Any results would only come after the next national election, due by mid-2029, and some in the next 10 years. For the time being, he asked the party at its annual conference in the northwestern English city of Liverpool to keep the faith. BURNHAM PROMISES 'NEW PATH' Walking on the stage to "All Together Now" by Liverpool band The Farm, Burnham said he had ignored his first instinct to give "the usual tub-thumping conference speech", instead deciding to offer "a more serious prospectus for Britain than people have been offered in a generation". It was a pitch decidedly aimed at the long term — aware of not only the lack of public money available to his new government but also the need to placate the bond markets, which have sent [USN:L8N45L0LP TEXT:"Britain's borrowing costs"] to high levels. His team said Burnham's speech and plan came from the heart, the culmination of his upbringing, his years spent at the centre of British politics in Westminster and those as Greater Manchester mayor. Burnham's main message of drawing "a line on a decade of division" to put "the country on a new path ... with hope again" was delivered with passion and well received by attendees. PROMISES TO STICK TO FISCAL RULES Labour lawmaker Peter Prinsley said he was optimistic. "I think it was a great boost to everybody, full of ideas and hope, but above all honest," he told Reuters. But even his most vocal supporters said a lot of his new prospectus, which included plans to change Britain's [USN:L8N45L1HU TEXT:"first-past-the-post voting system"] and to see if he could build a consensus around a better [USN:L8N45L1HL TEXT:"post-Brexit relationship with the EU"], would come after the expected 2029 election. Promising to boost social housing, get more of the around 1 million young people in unemployment back into work, tackle the social care crisis and possibly to bring water firms under public control, it was an ambitious plan he conceded would be held back in the short term by fiscal constraints. He called on Labour and Britain's voters to stick with him, saying he had worked hard since coming to power in July to offer them immediate "breathing space" by capping bus fares and removing value added tax from electricity bills. "I hope you will see it as a sign, a strong one, of our intent to get your bills and fares down as you wait for the bigger changes to come," he said. "I would love to go quickly, but I have to be honest about what the country can afford. I will stick to our fiscal rules to get borrowing and debt down," he said, referring to the rules that require the government to balance day-to-day spending with revenue by the end of the decade. EMOTIONAL OVER CARE SERVICE On housing, he promised to prioritise the construction of social housing and to empower local councils to seize unoccupied private homes, while on youth employment, he vowed to create a balanced education system for academic and technical routes. He promised to repeal a ban on the public ownership of water companies, saying people should no longer have to pay to clean up private firms' failings, when sewage is routinely dumped into the country's rivers and seas — something that would require legislation and could take some time. But it was on social care where his passion came through. He recounted his father's and his grandmother's experiences, describing his despair at his grandmother's treatment, especially when her "engagement ring (was) ripped from her finger and stolen in a care home". He said he would set up a National Care Service funded by [USN:L8N45L1CK TEXT:"altering the triple lock"] — which guarantees a state pension rise each year by whichever is highest among inflation, wage growth or 2.5% — a cornerstone of the welfare offer to older people. The populist Reform UK party seized on that, asking why pensioners were being "asked to be the first to make sacrifices". But it was the description of his ultimate vision for Britain that caught in his throat. He described being told by Scotland's first minister, John Swinney, that he "would be the last prime minister of the United Kingdom" on the day his dad died. "The United Kingdom my dad represented is the one I believe in," he said, with tears in his eyes. "So I'm going to use this job to build the kind of Britain my dad wanted to see."
